newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Cyprus talks set for a long haul, UN envoy says.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus talks set for a long haul, UN envoy says.

text.p: Rival Greek and Turkish Cypriot leaders, confined within a cozy Swiss hotel to talk peace with no escape from each other, face more negotiations on Tuesday with their U.N. mediator predicting a long haul.

As well as sitting in formal talks for five days, Glafcos Clerides and Rauf Denktash are due to spend free time together to get beyond the formality of documents, using techniques U.S. peacebroker Richard Holbrooke employed to end the war in Bosnia.

The pair, who have known and battled each other for nearly half a century since they were young, London-trained lawyers, put on a display of joviality as they opened the talks at an exclusive hotel above Lake Leman near Montreux on Monday.

"Excellent cuisine," Denktash, 73, complimented the hotel management before shaking hands with Clerides, 78, in their first meeting since a first round last month near New York aimed at reuniting Cyprus under a bi-zonal, bi-communal federation.

Officials from both sides talked down prospects for an immediate solution, and U.N. special Cyprus envoy Diego Cordovez, chairing the talks under a media blackout, advocated a step-by-step rather than an all-or-nothing approach.

Cordovez told reporters he did not expect a one-shot solution to the problems of the two communities -- estranged since 1963, three years after independence from Britain -- when a government representing both broke apart amid violence.
"In the past, they started from zero and ended with zero. They started from zero trying to get one hundred," he said.
Cyprus has been divided since 1974 when Turkey invaded its northern third in response to a coup in the capital Nicosia, backed by the military junta then ruling Greece.
Discussions on a U.N.-drafted paper calling for a sustained process of open-ended, direct talks start on Tuesday, but diplomats said neither side appeared ready to compromise.

Public positions have become more entrenched since the last talks. Stakes are higher with Cyprus preparing for entry talks with the European Union early next year and Turkey saying it will move towards partial integration with the north.
Among the key sticking points are Denktash`s insistence on sovereignty and the Greek Cypriot wish for free settlement.
Holbrooke, the international community`s trump card in the talks, is waiting on the sidelines to step in at the right moment with his tough, result-oriented diplomacy.

Denktash, in an interview on Sunday, insisted on absolute political equality with Clerides. He also accused the EU of getting in the way of a deal and threatened to pull out: "If the EU talks start, the intercommunal talks will stop and that will be the end of the matter," he said.
Cordovez put the immediate emphasis on keeping the two sides talking to each other rather than on substance.
"We are changing the procedure. It has to be an incremental thing where you go slowly building an agreement...I am not expecting them to solve the problems now," he said.
But he added: "I expect them to cooperate with me and particularly with themselves. It is in their interests."

Whether they like it or not, Denktash and Clerides have nowhere to hide from each other inside the marble halls of the turn-of-the-century Righi Vaudois hotel where the pair, each accompanied by two aides, are the only clients.
They are stuck together like a divorced couple must find a solution for the future of their children after decades of separation.
"It is like a nightmare scenario," said one diplomat.
The pair will have to sit down to breakfast together on a veranda amid red geraniums and with Swiss plainclothes police keeping watch from the bushes.
"If one finds the other in the breakfast room, they will have to sit down together. There is no one else to have breakfast with," said a senior Greek Cypriot official.
